Senses.Explanation: Bian He is the pre-Chan jade-bearer whom the corpus invokes through the uncut-jade story. The name is attested 90 times across 52 texts. In his Book of Serenity commentary, Wansong Xingxiu retells the defining event: Bian He found an uncut stone in a valley of Mount Jing, offered it to King Li of Chu, was told it was stone, and had one foot cut off. Chan interviews compress the story into answers such as “white jade without flaw; Bian He has his foot cut off” (白玉無瑕，卞和刖足). A student explicitly adopts the role by telling Touzi Datong, “I bring you the uncut jade and ask you to carve and polish it”; when Touzi Datong refuses it as beam material, the student says, “then Bian He has nowhere to emerge” (卞和無出身處). Yuanwu’s verse names the repeated offering and its cost: “laughable, Bian He presents the jade three times; even if honored, both feet are cut off” (卞和三獻玉，縱榮刖却一雙足). Danxia Zichun's verse draws its own comparison: “Mount Jing’s fine jade—why discern it? … Bian He had knowledge; the king of Chu rejected him” (卞和有智楚王嫌). Zen therefore deploys Bian He as the named bearer of unrecognized jade in answers, student self-comparison, verses, and case commentary. These records, not a general literary biography, define the entry.

Senses.Explanation: This is the title of the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra. A supplementary preface by Yang Jie reports that Yongming read it and gives ‘Buddha-speech takes mind as its source’; this non-master preface supports that public claim but does not count toward the depth floor. Guifeng Zongmi identifies a tathāgatagarbha statement as based on the scripture. Yuanwu says Mazu raised its ‘Buddha-speech takes mind as its source; no gate is the gateway’ line and then explains it. Wuyi Yuanlai cites that line in two independent recorded addresses, one before moving to other scriptures and one before asking where the assembly recognizes its own mind-ground. In an authored question Yongming raises the scripture's statement that quiescent true suchness has no sequence, while Weilin raises ‘prior sages knew it and transmitted it in turn’ and responds with a verse. Reading, citing, questioning, versifying, and explaining are different uses of the same titled work, not different meanings of the title.

Senses.Explanation: To ascend the teaching hall is to take the public teaching position before the assembly. Two master-authored works and five independent sayings records use the expression for entering the hall to address the community, give teaching, receive questions, or conduct a named public occasion. The action is institutional and public. It does not merely mean walking upstairs: speakers pair it with teaching, entering a private interview room, bells and drums, the gathered assembly, and the formal exchange of questions and answers. One early lamp biography is retained only as a supplemental recension showing its named subject ascending the hall, surveying the assembly, and speaking. It does not count toward the seven-work depth floor.

Senses.Explanation: “Not mind, not buddha” is Mazu's counter-saying after “mind itself is buddha”: it withdraws the positive formula once that formula has become something to cling to. In Mazu Daoyi's exchange, he says “mind itself is buddha” was used to stop a child's crying; when the crying stops, his answer is “not mind, not buddha.” Yongming Yanshou calls the phrase a negative or blocking exposition that removes error and attachment, but warns against treating negative language itself as final. Guifeng Zongmi likewise cites attachment to “not mind, not buddha” as the mistake of preferring negation while refusing to recognize what the words are used to uncover.

Senses.Explanation: The category fall is one of Caoshan's three falls and is explicitly identified with 'wearing fur and horns'; records contrast it with the following fall and the honored-position fall. Caoshan Benji answers the question 'what fall is wearing fur and horns?' with 'it is the category fall.' The same exchange separately assigns not cutting off sound and form to the following fall, and not accepting food to the honored-position fall. Yongjue Yuanxian and later Caodong teachers retain the three names as public interview questions but answer them with new verses or denials. Those later answers preserve the category as a named position without replacing Caoshan's explicit classification.
